strengths: The paper poses a clear and potentially useful question: which ViT components should be prioritized during selective finetuning. The component-wise perspective and average input-output sensitivity measure provide an intuitive lens that is reasonably original, even though related observations about attention-only or partial finetuning already exist.

The empirical study is extensive in raw scale: approximately 800 runs, four learning rates, three seeds, 11 reported benchmarks, comparisons with linear probing and full finetuning, and detailed optimization traces. The results consistently show that tuning attention or feedforward parameters is competitive with full finetuning and usually outperforms tuning LayerNorm alone.

Comparisons among MHA, FC1, and FC2 control the trainable-parameter count at approximately 28M each. The manuscript also reports means and standard deviations and applies a paired nonparametric test to aggregate comparisons.

The paper is generally well organized and visually polished. The main intuition, experimental configurations, hyperparameters, parameter counts, memory estimates, and limitations concerning vision-only evaluation and optimization choices are presented clearly.
The work has no apparent material ethical concern; the datasets and models are standard, and the impact statement is proportionate to the low-risk methodological contribution.
weaknesses: The central mathematical definition is not well-defined: Definition 1 invokes a uniform distribution over all distinct pairs in the unbounded continuous space (R^d)^n, for which no uniform probability distribution exists. The experiments instead use pairs drawn from ImageNet and downstream datasets, making the measured quantity distribution-dependent and different from the stated definition.

The claimed theoretical plasticity ranking does not follow from Propositions 1-4. Ordering loose upper bounds cannot establish an ordering of the underlying plasticities; the attention bound is acknowledged to be several orders of magnitude above the empirical values. The comparison further relies on informal assumptions that weights have entries in similar ranges and spectral norms exceed one, rather than a theorem. Consequently, the empirical ordering does not validate the theoretical argument in the claimed sense.

Proposition 1 assumes that every token at a fixed position has identical feature mean and standard deviation across all images. ImageNet input normalization and use of a shared patch embedding do not imply this. The explanation given for the assumption is therefore incorrect, so the LayerNorm bound does not apply to the stated experimental setting. The implementation also uses an epsilon of 1e-12 that is absent from the analysis.

The practical estimator is questionable and insufficiently specified. In particular, FC2 inputs are constructed by zero-padding d-dimensional tokens to 4d rather than using the actual GELU(FC1(.)) activations encountered by FC2. Thus components are not evaluated on their operational input distributions, undermining comparisons of their purported intrinsic plasticity. Pairing and sampling details needed to reproduce the 12,800-sample estimate are also missing.

The proposed mechanism linking input-output plasticity to finetuning is not established. No result connects this average secant ratio to parameter-gradient magnitude or downstream accuracy. The gradient evidence is heavily confounded: global gradient norms for 28M-parameter MHA/FC modules are compared against norms for 18K-parameter LayerNorm modules without normalization, while identical learning-rate grids and norm clipping are used. Correlation across five structurally different module types is not evidence that plasticity causes improved optimization.

The performance evidence is substantially weaker than the wording suggests. MHA exceeds FC1 by only 0.07 points on average and the difference is not significant; the ordering is violated on multiple individual datasets, with LN2 or LN1 best among selective methods on Gaussian Noise, Flowers102, and Pets. Five of the 11 tasks are correlated CIFAR-10 corruptions, and finetuning is tested only on one pretrained ViT-Base model. ViT-Huge is used only for the plasticity plots, where architecture, dimension, depth, weights, and sequence length all change simultaneously, so the larger attention value cannot specifically validate sequence-length dependence.

Practical significance is limited: the recommended configurations tune 33% of the model, whereas LayerNorm tunes 0.02%, yet the average accuracy difference is under one point. There are no equal-budget comparisons, modern PEFT baselines such as LoRA/adapters, or demonstrations that using the measure selects a better configuration on unseen architectures or tasks. The empirical observation that attention/feedforward tuning works well is also already documented in cited prior work.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and architecture details are useful, but the manuscript provides no code-release statement, precise checkpoint identifiers in readable form, complete plasticity-estimation procedure, or statistical treatment accounting for selecting the best learning rate. Reporting test accuracy after hyperparameter selection is also ambiguous about whether selection was strictly validation-only.

The limitations section omits the most consequential issues: invalid distributional definition, inapplicable LayerNorm assumption, loose-bound ordering, off-manifold FC2 evaluation, parameter-count/gradient-norm confounding, and the inability of observational results to establish the claimed causal mechanism. There are also numerous technical and editorial errors, including defining a Lipschitz constant with K<=0, repeated expressions f_att(x)-f_att(x) in proofs, inconsistent measure symbols, and duplicate 'Takeaway 2' numbering.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely practical question— which ViT components to prioritize during selective finetuning—and the component-wise framing is intuitive.

The empirical study is substantial in raw scale: five component configurations, four learning rates, three seeds, approximately 800 runs, 11 reported benchmarks, and comparisons with full finetuning and linear probing.
The appendix provides proofs, hyperparameters, per-dataset results, gradient/loss trajectories, and model details. The manuscript is generally polished and easy to navigate.
The observation that attention and feedforward components usually outperform LayerNorm-only tuning may be practically useful, even though the proposed explanation is not established.
weaknesses: The central quantity is not mathematically well-defined: Definition 1 assumes a uniform distribution over all distinct pairs in the unbounded continuous space (R^d)^n, but no such probability distribution exists. The experiments instead use pairs drawn from ImageNet and downstream datasets, defining a different, distribution-dependent quantity.

The theoretical results do not establish the claimed ranking. Comparing upper bounds—especially bounds that differ by several orders of magnitude—cannot determine the ordering of the underlying plasticities. The argument additionally assumes that matrix entries have comparable ranges and uses empirical observations about spectral norms rather than proving the ranking.

Key theoretical assumptions are unjustified or false for the stated setting. Proposition 1 assumes every token at a given position has the same feature mean and standard deviation across images; ImageNet input normalization does not imply this after patch embedding. The numerical attention bound substitutes an average token radius for the required uniform bound. Proposition 4 also omits complications such as the CLS token, positional embeddings, and embedding biases.

The proposed mechanism connecting input-output sensitivity to finetuning is unsupported. A high average input rate of change only lower-bounds a Lipschitz constant; it does not imply a large parameter Jacobian, large optimization gradients, or better generalization. The cited discussion does not supply such an implication for these transformer components.

The performance comparison is severely confounded by capacity: MHA, FC1, and FC2 each train about 28M parameters, whereas each LayerNorm configuration trains only 18K. Larger unnormalized gradient norms are likewise expected for parameter groups of radically different sizes. No matched-budget experiment or intervention that changes plasticity while holding the module and parameter count fixed is provided.

Even among the equal-sized modules, evidence for the precise ranking is weak: MHA and FC1 differ by only 0.1 average accuracy point, FC1 often wins, and FC2 wins on Sketch. Across all modules, lower-ranked LayerNorm configurations win on Gaussian Noise, Flowers102, and Pets. Thus the data support a coarse MHA/MLP-versus-LayerNorm capacity distinction more clearly than the claimed monotonic plasticity law.

The plasticity computation itself is questionable. It evaluates ImageNet/downstream pairs rather than the defined distribution, and FC2 is tested using zero-padded embedded tokens rather than its actual post-GeLU hidden activations. This artificial, coordinate-dependent construction need not characterize FC2 in the operating transformer.

The ViT-Huge comparison changes architecture, depth, patch size, and sequence length simultaneously, so its higher attention plasticity cannot validate sequence-length dependence. Finetuning benefits are evaluated only on ViT-Base, one pretrained model family, and one optimizer protocol.

Statistical support is limited. Five corruption datasets plus CIFAR-10 share a common underlying source and should not be treated as six independent benchmarks in a Wilcoxon test. The paper reports no p-values or multiple-comparison correction, selects the best learning rate, and uses only three seeds. The claimed robustness also pools deliberately different learning rates and may instead reflect whether the fixed grid suits each parameterization.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no executable code or availability statement is provided; the deterministic split indices, exact seeds, plasticity pairing procedure, batch counts, and compute requirements are missing. The table caption promises pretrained-weight links, but none are visibly reported.

Presentation contains consequential imprecision: Lipschitz continuity is incorrectly introduced with K <= 0, expansion with plasticity above one is called 'non-smooth' despite not implying mathematical nonsmoothness, and two conclusions are both labeled Takeaway 2.

The limitations section discusses only future extensions and does not acknowledge the invalid population definition, loose-bound ranking, parameter-count confounding, or narrow model coverage. Ethical risk is low for this basic methodological study, but the impact statement is boilerplate rather than a substantive assessment. Overall, the empirical observation has merit, but the paper's main theoretical and causal claims are not supported strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper asks a practically relevant question— which ViT components should be prioritized during selective fine-tuning—and introduces an intuitive average rate-of-change perspective connecting component behavior to adaptation.

The empirical study is substantial: approximately 800 fine-tuning runs, 11 classification benchmarks, four learning rates, three seeds, and analyses of accuracy, variability, gradients, and validation loss. Comparisons between MHA, FC1, and FC2 are especially informative because these configurations have matched parameter counts.

The experiments reveal a reasonably consistent descriptive pattern: attention and feed-forward components have higher measured sensitivity and generally outperform LayerNorm-only tuning, with the largest differences on Cifar100, Clipart, and Sketch. The comparison to full fine-tuning and linear probing adds useful context.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear, provides proofs and extensive per-dataset training curves, and documents architectures, preprocessing, optimization, parameter counts, and memory estimates. The limitations section appropriately identifies the restriction to vision encoders and the lack of tailored optimization.

The component-level perspective is original and potentially useful for motivating future selective or low-rank adaptation methods. No material ethical concern is apparent for the image-classification experiments.
weaknesses: The formal definition is not mathematically well posed: Definition 1 invokes a uniform distribution over all distinct pairs in the unbounded continuous space of token sequences, for which no uniform probability distribution exists. The experiments instead use pairs drawn from specific pretraining and downstream datasets, so the measured quantity is distribution-dependent and does not instantiate the stated definition.

The claimed theoretical ranking does not follow from the propositions. The paper derives separate upper bounds, but a larger or looser upper bound for one component does not imply that its actual plasticity is larger. This is particularly problematic because Figure 6 shows the attention bound to be orders of magnitude looser than the observed rates. Assumptions such as comparable weight-entry scales and spectral norms above one do not repair this inference.

Proposition 1 relies on every token at a fixed position having the same feature-wise mean and standard deviation across inputs. ImageNet input normalization and a shared embedding layer do not imply this property for image patches or internal activations. Consequently, the LayerNorm bound is not shown to apply to the evaluated ViTs.

The empirical plasticity construction is questionable for FC2: Appendix C.4 pads d-dimensional tokens with zeros to create 4d-dimensional inputs, rather than evaluating FC2 on its actual GeLU(FC1) activations. This arbitrary embedding can materially affect both numerator and denominator, undermining the cross-component ranking.

The central causal interpretation is under-supported. Module identity simultaneously changes function, location, parameter count, representation distribution, and optimization geometry. In particular, MHA/FC configurations tune about 28M parameters while LayerNorm configurations tune only 18K, a roughly 1500-fold difference. The results therefore do not isolate plasticity as the reason for better performance. An intervention that changes plasticity while holding the component and parameter budget fixed, or stronger controlled analyses, is needed.

Several purported validations are confounded. ViT-Base and ViT-Huge differ in model size, depth, width, head count, patch size, weights, and sequence length, so their comparison cannot specifically validate sequence-length dependence. Likewise, fixed learning-rate grids and gradient clipping complicate the claim that larger gradients intrinsically produce faster or more robust optimization.

Table 6 reports the best test accuracy over the learning-rate grid. Although checkpoints are selected by validation accuracy within a run, the manuscript does not state that the learning rate itself is selected using validation data; as written, this constitutes test-set model selection and can inflate results. The average improvements are also small—about 0.1 points between MHA and FC1 and about 1 point between MHA and LayerNorm—and the asserted ordering has multiple per-dataset reversals.

Reproducibility is only partial: many implementation details and curves are supplied, but no anonymized code or complete specification of data splits, sampled image pairs, and plasticity computation is provided. Mathematical and editorial errors—including the Lipschitz constant being stated as K≤0, inconsistent notation in proofs, and duplicated “Takeaway 2”—also warrant correction.

The limitations discussion is honest but omits the most consequential limitations: the ill-defined reference distribution, looseness of the theoretical bounds, parameter-count confounding, artificial FC2 inputs, and possible test-set hyperparameter selection. Overall, the empirical observations are promising, but the present evidence does not support the paper’s central theoretical and causal claims strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes an intuitive and potentially useful perspective: comparing transformer components through average input-output sensitivity and relating it to selective finetuning. Applying this component-wise lens to transfer learning is reasonably original, even though the individual mathematical tools are standard.

The empirical study is unusually extensive: approximately 1,000 runs across 11 vision benchmarks, four learning rates, three seeds, and five component groups. Additional experiments cover Adam, a 1,000-example regime, ViT-Large, and plasticity measurements on DINOv3 and GPT-2.

The main empirical observation is consistent at a descriptive level: tuning attention or feedforward layers generally outperforms tuning LayerNorm parameters. Table 8 reports average accuracies of 90.75/90.68/90.31 for MHA/FC1/FC2 versus 89.93/89.82 for LN2/LN1.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with useful diagrams, full per-dataset results, optimization traces, architecture details, hyperparameters, memory estimates, and an extensive appendix.

Reproducibility is supported by detailed preprocessing and optimization protocols, pretrained-model specifications, learning-rate grids, and a carbon-footprint estimate. The work raises no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The central definition is not mathematically well-defined: Definition 1 invokes a uniform distribution over all distinct pairs in the unbounded continuous space (R^d)^n, but no such probability distribution exists. The experiments instead use ImageNet and downstream images, so the formal quantity and empirical estimator do not correspond without specifying a valid pair distribution.

The claimed theoretical ranking does not follow from the propositions. Comparing upper bounds—especially bounds with very different looseness—cannot establish an ordering of the underlying plasticities. The attention bound being orders of magnitude larger may merely reflect its looseness. The argument additionally assumes comparable weight-entry scales, spectral norms above one, and favorable normalization statistics without establishing conditions sufficient for the stated ranking.

Proposition 1 relies on every token at a given position having the same feature mean and standard deviation across input sequences. ImageNet input normalization and use of a shared embedding layer do not imply this; patch contents cause these statistics to vary by image. Thus the LayerNorm result does not apply to the practical setting used to support the paper's principal comparison.

The empirical plasticity construction is questionable. Appendix D.3 says components are applied to embedded image tokens, and FC2 inputs are manufactured by zero-padding d-dimensional tokens to 4d. These are not FC2's actual inputs, which are GeLU(FC1(LN2(hidden states))), nor are raw patch embeddings generally the actual inputs to components in deeper blocks. Consequently, the measured ranking may primarily reflect operator scales under an artificial input distribution rather than operational sensitivity inside the transformer.

The experiments do not identify plasticity as the cause of improved finetuning. MHA, FC1, and FC2 each expose about 28M trainable parameters, whereas each LayerNorm group exposes only 18K, so the high-plasticity/low-plasticity comparison is almost perfectly confounded by adaptation capacity. Equal-parameter random subsets, matched-rank adapters, or interventions that change a component's plasticity while holding its trainable capacity fixed are absent.

Even among the three equally sized groups, the proposed ordering is not consistently predictive: FC1 beats MHA on Cifar10 and Cifar100, FC2 is best on Sketch, and low-plasticity modules are best on Gaussian Noise, Flowers102, and Pets in Table 8. The paper supplies neither correlations between measured plasticity and accuracy across datasets/layers/models nor a statistical test of the overall monotonic relationship.

The link from input sensitivity to parameter-gradient magnitude and then to better optimization is asserted rather than established. Raw gradient norms are not directly comparable across parameter groups with radically different dimensions and parameterizations, and larger gradients do not by themselves imply better generalization. The selected optimization traces and observational alignment cannot establish the proposed mechanism.

The practical significance is limited because the main actionable result—attention and large feedforward matrices usually outperform LayerNorm-only tuning—is already plausible from parameter count and consistent with cited prior empirical work. No new finetuning algorithm is developed, and the paper does not show that plasticity selects modules better than simpler baselines such as trainable parameter count, weight norm, or validation-based selection.

The limitations section mentions only optimizer tailoring and future LLM experiments; it does not acknowledge the invalid probability definition, restrictive LayerNorm assumption, artificial FC2 inputs, unequal parameter budgets, or correlational nature of the evidence. These are central limitations rather than minor scope qualifications.

strengths: The paper asks a useful practical question— which transformer components should be prioritized during selective finetuning—and evaluates five component types across 11 image-classification settings, multiple learning rates and seeds, SGD and Adam, low-data experiments, and several ViT scales.

The empirical observation that attention and feedforward components generally outperform LayerNorm-only tuning is potentially useful. Table 8 includes full-finetuning and linear-probing references, and the appendices provide extensive training curves and implementation details.
Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with effective figures and a readable progression from the proposed measure to theory and experiments.
The paper reports computational cost and estimated carbon emissions. The work has no evident major ethical risk beyond compute usage.
weaknesses: The central definition is mathematically ill-posed: there is no uniform probability distribution over all distinct pairs in the unbounded continuous space (R^d)^n. The experiments instead use pairs drawn from particular pretraining and downstream datasets, making plasticity distribution-dependent and inconsistent with Definition 1.

The claimed theoretical ranking does not follow from the propositions. Comparing upper bounds—especially bounds of radically different looseness—cannot establish an ordering of the underlying plasticities. The attention bound is acknowledged to be orders of magnitude looser, so its larger value provides essentially no evidence that attention has larger plasticity.

Proposition 1 assumes every token at a position has the same feature mean and standard deviation across inputs. Image normalization does not imply this, particularly for hidden tokens in deeper blocks. Consequently, the LayerNorm bound does not characterize the modules evaluated experimentally.

Proposition 4 bounds tokens using only the patch-embedding operator and image energy, but attention modules in later blocks receive representations altered by earlier attention, MLP, residual, positional, and normalization operations. CLS and positional embeddings are also omitted. Thus its assumptions do not justify the stated bound for internal ViT attention modules.

The empirical plasticity computation is poorly aligned with actual module operation. In particular, FC2 inputs are constructed by zero-padding d-dimensional tokens to 4d rather than using the genuine GeLU(FC1(.)) activations. More generally, the description does not establish that each module is evaluated on its true layer-specific input distribution, so the reported ranking may largely reflect weight norms and artificial inputs.

The finetuning comparison severely confounds plasticity with capacity and parameterization: MHA/FC configurations train about 28M parameters, whereas each LayerNorm configuration trains only 18K. The reported global gradient norms are likewise not comparable across groups with roughly 1,500-fold different parameter counts and distinct Jacobian structures. No matched-budget, within-module plasticity intervention, or controlled regression establishes that plasticity—rather than parameter count, architecture, or scaling—causes the optimization and accuracy differences.

The purported validation of sequence-length dependence compares ViT-Base and ViT-Huge, changing model size, depth, width, heads, patching, and weights simultaneously. It does not isolate sequence length.

The evidence is weaker than the repeated claim of consistent superiority suggests. In Table 8, the aggregate gap between MHA and LN2 is only about 0.8 points; LayerNorm variants win on some datasets, and MHA is not consistently best even among high-plasticity components. Five of the 11 benchmarks are correlated CIFAR-10-C variants, weakening averages and the Wilcoxon analysis; multiple comparisons are not addressed.

Model selection is ambiguous: Table 8 says it reports the best test accuracy over the learning-rate grid, while the protocol only states that checkpoints are selected by validation accuracy. If learning rates were selected using test accuracy, this biases the results; if not, the validation-based learning-rate selection procedure should be specified.

Originality is limited. The proposed quantity is an elementary expected secant slope, the bounds largely adapt standard Lipschitz arguments, and the practical value of attention-only tuning was already documented by cited prior work. A meaningful new explanatory result would require a valid theory and experiments that isolate the proposed factor.

Reproducibility is mixed: many hyperparameters, seeds, dataset splits, and parameter counts are supplied, but the exact sampling/pairing procedure for plasticity, some sample/batch details, and several cross-architecture settings are insufficiently specified. Full replication also requires approximately 3,700 GPU-hours.

The limitations section only mentions optimizer tailoring and future LLM work. It does not acknowledge the distribution dependence and ill-posed definition, looseness of the bounds, unrealistic assumptions, off-manifold FC2 evaluation, parameter-count confounding, correlated benchmarks, or the lack of causal evidence. These unresolved issues undermine the paper's central theoretical and empirical claims and prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper offers an interesting perspective on selective finetuning by relating transformer components' input-output sensitivity to their adaptability. If validated more rigorously, this could provide useful guidance for parameter-efficient adaptation.

Empirical breadth: The study reports roughly 1,000 finetuning runs across 11 classification benchmarks, multiple learning rates and seeds, SGD and Adam, a low-data setting, and several ViT scales. The descriptive plasticity pattern is also checked on DINOv3 and GPT-2.

Useful controls: MHA, FC1, and FC2 have approximately equal trainable parameter counts, as do LN1 and LN2, permitting some comparisons that are not explained solely by parameter count. Full finetuning and linear probing are also reported.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished. The appendix documents preprocessing, optimization, trainable parameters, memory use, model configurations, and per-dataset results in substantial detail.

Reproducibility and ethics: Hyperparameter grids, training schedules, data splits, and checkpoint selection are described, and the authors report compute use and estimated carbon emissions. I found no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 1 is not mathematically well-defined: there is no uniform probability distribution over all distinct pairs in the unbounded continuous space (R^d)^n. Plasticity must instead be defined relative to an explicit probability distribution, which would also make clear that it is distribution-dependent rather than an intrinsic property of a component.

The theoretical results do not establish the claimed plasticity ranking. Ordering loose upper bounds does not imply an ordering of the underlying quantities. The appendix itself shows an attention upper bound several orders of magnitude above the observed plasticity, emphasizing that the bound is not quantitatively informative.

Proposition 1 relies on all samples' tokens at a given position having identical feature-wise mean and standard deviation. ImageNet input normalization and use of a shared embedding layer do not imply this assumption, contrary to the manuscript's justification. Thus the LayerNorm result is not shown to apply to the evaluated models.

The proposed connection to finetuning is correlational rather than causal. No experiment changes plasticity while holding component identity, parameterization, capacity, and optimization fixed. Consequently, the observed five-component ordering cannot establish that plasticity itself causes better optimization or generalization.

The empirical plasticity comparison uses embedded image tokens as common inputs to components that encounter different activation distributions inside the actual network; FC2 is evaluated using an especially artificial zero-padding of d-dimensional tokens to 4d rather than its real GeLU(FC1) inputs. Rates of change across different domains, codomains, and representation scales are not directly comparable and are sensitive to function-preserving rescalings of adjacent layers.

The strongest high-versus-low plasticity comparison is heavily confounded by capacity: MHA/FC1/FC2 each train about 28M parameters, whereas each LayerNorm configuration trains only 18K. Likewise, raw parameter-gradient norms mechanically depend on parameter count and scaling. Parameter-budget-matched subsets and normalized update or gradient measures are needed. Among the equal-size high-plasticity modules, performance differences are small and frequently do not follow the proposed order on individual datasets.

Evaluation protocol concerns remain: Table 8 reports the best test accuracy over the learning-rate grid, rather than clearly selecting the learning rate exclusively by validation performance before evaluating the test set. Some other tables instead average over learning rates. This inconsistent aggregation complicates both performance and robustness claims.

Scope is narrower than the framing suggests. Five of the 11 benchmarks are corruptions of CIFAR-10, and actual finetuning evidence is almost entirely for supervised pretrained ViTs; DINOv3 and GPT-2 receive only descriptive plasticity measurements. The claim of general guidance for transformers or LLMs is therefore premature.

Reproducibility is limited by the very high reported cost (3,700 GPU-hours), custom benchmark splits without indices in the manuscript, and the absence of a usable code location in the anonymized copy. The limitations section does not acknowledge the undefined distribution, looseness of the bounds, artificial FC2 inputs, parameter-count confounding, or the lack of a causal intervention.

Overall, the empirical regularity is promising and the paper is well presented, but the central theoretical and mechanistic claims are not currently supported. Correcting the definition, reframing the upper bounds, and adding controlled, parameter-matched interventions would be necessary before others could reliably build on the claimed principle.
